extracted.intended_audience: general readers of satirical Renaissance literature (readers of Rabelais)
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from François Rabelais's Gargantua — comic/satirical prose mixing bodily humor, mock-learned rhetoric, and a (satiric) set of prescriptions about education, manners, and bodily practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of an admirable praise/oration
rubrics_metrics.description: The successful complimentary speech (as exemplified by Eudemon) is delivered with proper gestures, distinct pronunciation, pleasant delivery, exquisite fine terms, and 'so good Latin' that the speaker seems a Gracchus, Cicero, or Aemilius rather than a youth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and surrounding guidance: stand up straight, cap in hand, maintain a clear and open countenance, steady eyes, modest looks, and use graceful pronunciation and tasteful diction. The passage contrasts this model of polished oratory with the grotesque, bumbling pedantry of the sophister Janotus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-fold virtues to praise in a youth (structure of encomium)
rubrics_metrics.description: When commending a young man, give praise in ordered points: (1) for his virtue and good manners; (2) for his knowledge; (3) for his nobility; (4) for his bodily accomplishments; (5) exhort him to reverence his father — the five places Eudemon used in addressing Gargantua.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivered sweetly and in humble tone; this list models the content and sequence of an effective complimentary speech in the social/moral code of the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid antiquated scholastic curricula that 'bastardize' youth
rubrics_metrics.description: Rabelais critiques the traditional sophistic curriculum as 'nothing but brutishness' and 'blunt foppish toys' that make pupils 'foolish, simple, doted, and blockish' rather than wiser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: prefer instruction that actually produces better judgment, better discourse expressed in better terms, and civility of carriage — otherwise 'it were better for him to learn nothing at all.' The text treats rote study of useless authorities as an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select tutors fit to the pupil's capacity and promise
rubrics_metrics.description: When a child's natural understanding is evident, commit him 'to some learned man, to have him indoctrinated according to his capacity' and 'spare no cost' — modelled after Grangousier's decision to appoint a skilled preceptor when he recognizes Gargantua's gifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy invoked: Philip choosing Aristotle for Alexander; guidance is to match tutor calibre to pupil promise and to ensure instruction is appropriate (not merely traditional or low-quality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily regimen of the Sophisters (prescriptive/satiric school routine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sophisters' prescribed routine: wake ordinarily between eight and nine o'clock (whether day or not), tumble and toss and wallow in bed to stir up 'vital spirits', apparel according to season, comb with an 'Almain comb' (the four fingers and the thumb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the discipline imposed by the old governors; Rabelais uses it both as descriptive prescription and satirical commentary on pedantic notions of discipline (e.g., the preceptor claiming washing and making neat is 'to lose time in this world').

rubrics_metrics.name: Best torchecul (wipe-breech): goose-neck standard
rubrics_metrics.description: After trying many materials, Gargantua claims 'there is none in the world comparable to the neck of a goose, that is well downed, if you hold her head betwixt your legs' as the most 'lordly, excellent, and convenient' means to wipe one's bum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale offered: softness of the down and the temperate heat of the goose transmit pleasant warmth to the 'bum-gut' and inner regions; this is presented as the pinnacle/criterion of torchecul quality and even a key to Elysian felicity (tongue-in-cheek).

rubrics_metrics.name: Torchecul anti-patterns and harms to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Several wiping materials are shown to be harmful: golden spangles on satin 'fetched away all the skin', a March-cat's claws 'scratched and exulcerated' the perineum, and some remedies (mercury, parsley, nettles) produced illnesses like the 'bloody flux of Lombardy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit rule: avoid abrasive, sharp, or toxic materials; prefer soft, non-irritating, and pleasantly scented options (e.g., mother's gloves with Arabian Benin perfume helped recovery). The sequence of failures functions as negative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical and petition anti-pattern: bombastic, incoherent sophistry
rubrics_metrics.description: Janotus de Bragmardo's oration is a parody of bad rhetoric: coughing and gibberish, irrelevant boasting, mixed and mangled Latin, self-serving promises, circumlocution, and incoherent erudition — demonstrating how not to argue or petition effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-guidance implicit in the text: avoid overblown learned jargon, mixed register, obscure citations without purpose, self-interest presented as public good, and rambling incoherence; these undermine persuasion and provoke ridicule.
